kp.k: Advisory platform connects private capital with UK legal opportunities
kp.d: The article reports that former Allen & Overy managing partners Wim Dejonghe and David Morley launched Dejonghe & Morley to advise private equity investors entering the UK legal sector. Its stated aim is to bridge law firms and investors and support more sustainable private capital partnerships.
qs: Wim Dejonghe and David Morley, both past managing partners at the magic circle firm – now merged into A&O Shearman – have unveiled Dejonghe & Morley, a boutique advisory platform focused on matching capital with legal sector opportunities.
The founders of Dejonghe & Morley aim to support more sustainable private capital partnerships by leveraging their leadership experience to bridge the gap between law firms and investors.

kp.k: Scaling and AI investment accompany rising private equity interest
kp.d: The article links growing investor interest to law firms' high margins and pressure to scale, invest in AI and digitise delivery. It reports that CVC, Cinven and Permira are evaluating legal opportunities, explicitly noting that they have not publicly commented. It presents private equity activity in accounting, including Cinven's Grant Thornton investment, as an adjacent-sector parallel rather than evidence of AI's realised effects.
qs: The move comes amid rising private equity interest in professional services, particularly law firms, as investors seek exposure to a high-margin sector increasingly under pressure to scale operations, invest in AI, and digitise service delivery.
CVC, Cinven, and Permira are among the buyout firms reportedly evaluating opportunities in the legal space, although they have not publicly commented.
The trend mirrors growing activity in adjacent sectors, such as private equity's recent entry into the accounting industry, including Cinven's investment in Grant Thornton.

kp.k: Founders predict more transactions and private equity competition
kp.d: Dejonghe and Morley predict more law firm–investment firm transactions within the next 12 to 18 months. Morley further anticipates that every firm will eventually compete with some form of private equity model. These are forward-looking views, not reported market outcomes.
qs: Dejonghe and Morley believe that more transactions between law firms and investment firms will emerge in the next 12 to 18 months.
"Firms have strategic choices to make. Before long, I think every firm is going to find themselves competing with some kind of private equity model," said Morley.

kp.k: Acquisitions illustrate appetite for scalable legal assets
kp.d: The article cites Inflexion's £342m take-private acquisition of DWF in 2023 and Investcorp's acquisition of Stowe as examples of private equity investment in UK law firms. It interprets these transactions as suggesting demand for scalable legal assets aligned with digital innovation, without establishing that AI caused the deals.
qs: Inflexion took UK law firm DWF private in a £342m deal in 2023, while Investcorp acquired UK family law firm Stowe.
These transactions suggest growing appetite for scalable legal assets aligned with digital innovation.

kp.k: Dejonghe predicts AI will challenge leverage and hourly rates
kp.d: Dejonghe identifies AI as a catalyst for structural change and predicts business-model disruption at an unspecified future point. He warns that firms failing to engage with AI's potential impact while continuing to rely on staffing leverage and hourly rates will lose competitively; the article provides no measured operational effects.
qs: Dejonghe, who led the A&O merger with Shearman & Sterling, highlighted artificial intelligence as a catalyst for structural change.
"At some point AI will change the business model," he said.
"If you don't engage with the potential impact and keep working with leverage and hourly rates, you'll ultimately lose out in the market."

kp.k: Non-lawyer ownership has had mixed uptake
kp.d: The article qualifies the investment opportunity by noting mixed uptake after the UK opened its legal market to non-lawyer ownership over a decade earlier. It cites RBG Holdings' 2025 delisting following governance and funding challenges as a cautionary example, not as an AI-related outcome.
qs: While the UK opened its legal market to non-lawyer ownership over a decade ago, the uptake has been mixed.
RBG Holdings, one of the early listed law firms, delisted in 2025 following governance and funding challenges.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Wim Dejonghe predicts that AI will change law firms' business model and that firms which retain leverage and hourly billing without engaging with AI's potential impact will lose competitively.
pts.d: Dejonghe presents AI as a catalyst for structural change rather than identifying particular tasks it will automate. His warning concerns continued reliance on staffing leverage and hourly rates without adaptation; it does not specify a replacement business model. Separately, the article frames pressure to invest in AI, scale operations and digitise delivery as part of the context for increasing private equity interest in law firms. The prediction by Dejonghe and David Morley of more investment transactions is a related legal-market forecast, not an explicit claim that AI alone will cause those transactions.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The AI business-model forecast rests on Dejonghe's professional authority; the article offers investment examples as market context, not measurements of AI's effects.
pts.d: The article identifies Dejonghe as a former Allen & Overy managing partner who led its merger with Shearman & Sterling. It supplies no AI performance data, quantified productivity effects or demonstrated causal link between AI adoption and competitive outcomes. Inflexion's acquisition of DWF and Investcorp's acquisition of Stowe illustrate private capital activity; they do not establish that AI drove those deals. The article also notes RBG Holdings' governance and funding difficulties, qualifying the broader account of outside ownership rather than testing the AI prediction.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: AI-driven business-model change has no specified deadline; competitive loss is conditional on failing to engage with AI while retaining existing leverage and hourly rates.
pts.d: Dejonghe uses the indefinite terms 'At some point' and 'ultimately'. The article describes investment and digitisation pressure as already increasing. Its separate 12-to-18-month forecast, reported in this 2025 article, concerns transactions between law firms and investment firms, not the timing of AI-driven business-model change. Morley's forecast of widespread competition with private equity models is likewise expressed without a precise deadline.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claims concern law firms' competitive position, staffing and pricing models, and private equity investors seeking UK legal-sector opportunities.
pts.d: Within the article's UK market focus, law firms face pressure to fund AI investment and digitise service delivery. Dejonghe's warning particularly implicates firms relying on non-partner-to-partner staffing leverage and hourly billing without engaging with AI's implications. Private equity investors are presented as seeking opportunities in scalable legal businesses. The source does not specify consequences for individual lawyer roles, employment levels, client prices or access to justice.
